SEC27A-01.note: 'a sheltered block ... flowered eleven days later' is an independent clause, so a semicolon joins the two clauses. A is attractive because 'orchard, a sheltered block...' reads as an appositive until the verb 'flowered' arrives; colon fails since clause 2 does not explain clause 1.

SEC27A-02.note: Head noun 'milk' is singular; present tense required by 'comes back' and the standing rule. 'quarter'/'cows'' and the past 'injected' pull toward B/A.

SEC27A-03.note: Cataphoric ellipsis of 'has trouble sprouting' needs the do-auxiliary, plural for 'samples': 'rarely do'. 'rarely have' tempts by echoing main-verb 'has (trouble)', but ellipsis of lexical have takes do in American usage.

SEC27A-04.note: 'A booster given months after the others ... turned out to raise' is a new independent clause, so a sentence break is needed. A/D tempt by reading the booster as an appositive to 'dose', which leaves 'turned out' with no subject.

SEC27A-05.note: Plural head 'probes'; 'for nine growing seasons' requires present perfect progressive. C ('are measuring') is the tense trap.

SEC27A-06.note: Compound subject (veterinarian and technicians) takes 'have'; 'their' refers to the chicks/birds. 'its' could be tempting for the flock/grower, but 'flock' is only a modifier and the birds are plural.

SEC27A-07.note: 'Certain species' is plural (determiner 'certain'); present tense required by 'is not planted'. 'species' looks singular and 'row' sits right before the blank, pulling toward A.

SEC27A-08.note: 'found' takes the clause 'the hand-rub bottles ... were used' as its object; no punctuation between a verb and its object clause. Dash/comma tempt because the object clause is long.

SEC27A-09.note: Ellipsis of 'is dependable' (from 'are ... hardly dependable'); singular 'program' takes 'is'. 'does' tempts if the elided predicate is misread as a lexical verb.

SEC27A-10.note: One graft, 'the final join of a long career' = one person: singular possessive. D tempts through the plural 'propagators' earlier in the passage.

SEC27B-01.note: Restrictive participle: the passage contrasts these specimens with those from the frozen interior, so 'gathered where...' identifies which specimens; no punctuation. A/C (comma, single dash) are grammatical but nonrestrictive and leave 'the specimens' unidentified; this is a meaning-based call, the weakest point of exclusivity.

SEC27B-02.note: Plural 'readings'; past because the landing stage is long demolished. 'pier' sits before the blank pulling toward singular; 'are taken' is the tense trap.

SEC27B-03.note: Present 'marks the first time that' takes present perfect; singular 'filter bank' ('bays' is the attractor). C ('was superseded') is colloquially heard and is the main risk to exclusivity, but the convention with present 'marks/is the first time' is present perfect.

SEC27B-04.note: 'has always ... subsided' (present perfect, participle 'subsided' eight words later); singular 'level'. 'is always' tempts because the blank reads like a linking verb until 'subsided' is found.

SEC27B-05.note: An earthquake has one epicenter, so 'located beneath a shallow bay' is nonrestrictive and set off by a comma. A tempts as the plain option; colon does not introduce a participial phrase.

SEC27B-06.note: Singular 'dish' takes 'is'; the agent is the motors ('No motor working alone...'), so 'them'. 'it' tempts via nearby singular nouns (reflector, telescope).

SEC27B-07.note: Singular 'drive'; past because the duty is now obsolete. 'prisms' attracts plural; 'is being' is the tense trap.

SEC27B-08.note: 'surges' is a plural NOUN here (subject 'overflow surges'), and the result persists ('which is why ... sits'), so present perfect 'have carved'. Readers who parse 'surges' as the verb pick the singular A.

SEC27B-09.note: Plural 'wires', past narration ('wedged'), predicate adjective 'brittle' needs be: 'were also'. 'have/has also' fail only once 'brittle' is found past the intervening phrase.

SEC27B-10.convention: close apposition: a common-noun title directly before a proper name ('the ship Kittiwake Star') is conventionally unpunctuated even when the referent is unique
SEC27B-10.note: The opening sentence establishes the institute used one ship, so the name is nonrestrictive and can be set off; a single dash running to the period does so, with 'a trawler...' appositive to the name. D breaks the name 'Kittiwake Star'; C is a fragment.
SEC27B-10.drop_reason: Not exclusive: close apposition ('the institute's ship Kittiwake Star') is a recognised unpunctuated form, and the key depends on reading uniqueness of ownership into 'the same ship'.

SEC27C-01.note: Introductory 'While the organist played' ends before 'the pipes', which is the main-clause subject of 'sounded'; comma after 'played'. B/C garden-path 'played the pipes' as verb+object, leaving the main clause subjectless.

SEC27C-02.note: Singular 'portrait'; present because of the habitual 'whenever ... crowd'. 'donors'' attracts plural, 'began ... last spring' attracts past.

SEC27C-03.note: Plural 'bronzes'; 'since the museum opened' requires present perfect. 'temple'/'collector's' attract singular.

SEC27C-04.note: 'then a second mask, its pale cheeks...' is a noun phrase continuing the depiction, not a clause; 'then' is an adverb, so a comma. A tempts via the 'semicolon before then' rule, which needs an independent clause after it.

SEC27C-05.note: Plural 'copies' takes 'follow'; the object is the single borrowed psalter, so 'it'. 'novices'/'misspellings' tempt 'them'.

SEC27C-06.note: Singular 'helper'; past because 'caught fire'. 'projectionists'' attracts plural; present options clash with the narration.
SEC27C-06.drop_reason: Too easy for the module-2 hard route: one clear attractor, a plain past cue and weak distractors.

SEC27C-07.note: Plural 'tracks'; a specific past time ('on the night of the club's closing concert') takes simple past, not present perfect. D tempts by echoing 'have circulated since'.

SEC27C-08.note: Compound subject (warden and clerk) is plural; the verb completes as progressive 'are ... recording' (seven words later), so 'are', not 'do' (which would need 'record').

SEC27C-09.note: 'the sheet' is the object of 'proofread'; the introductory clause ends after it and 'pressmen ... were forbidden' is the main clause. A tempts because 'proofread' can be intransitive.

SEC27C-10.note: 'chart' is the main verb and the blank is its subject; plural 'historians' agrees with base 'chart'. C/D tempt by reading 'historian's chart corrections' as a noun phrase, which leaves the sentence without a verb.

SEC27D-01.note: A colon after a complete clause introduces the list of household types. A comma is attractive but makes the list read ambiguously as part of a series; semicolon leaves a fragment.

SEC27D-02.note: Plural 'loans'; present because 'a scarcity that keeps'. 'title'/'farmer' attract singular; the past survey frame attracts 'were rare'.

SEC27D-03.note: Plural 'cashiers'; the paper-ticket years are over, so past progressive, not present perfect. 'system's' attracts singular.

SEC27D-04.note: Ellipsis of 'crept upward' from 'has crept upward' needs 'have'; plural 'hours'. 'outlet'/'highway' attract singular C; 'are too' fails because the elided element is a participle.

SEC27D-05.note: 'ruled out' is a phrasal verb whose object is 'raising the residential water rate again'; no punctuation between verb and object. Dash/comma tempt by reading 'raising...' as an appended phrase.

SEC27D-06.note: Singular 'registrar'; 'it' refers to the family's single questionnaire. 'answers'/'family' plural-looking nouns tempt 'were/them'.

SEC27D-07.note: Singular 'turnout'; past because of 'during the mayoral runoff that autumn'. 'renters'/'blocks' attract plural; present perfect clashes with the bounded past time.

SEC27D-08.note: Singular 'teacher', present to parallel 'borrows'. 'dialects' attracts plural; past forms clash.
SEC27D-08.drop_reason: Too easy for the module-2 hard route: a single attractor ('dialects') and present parallel to 'borrows' with weak distractors.

SEC27D-09.note: A colon after the complete clause 'where the planners had expected it least' introduces the elaborating noun phrase. Semicolon leaves a fragment; A/C run 'least outlying' together.

SEC27D-10.convention: attributive noun: 'the contractor tally' is a legitimate noun-adjunct compound that is number-neutral (like 'the worker tally'); flagged as a possible second, low confidence
SEC27D-10.note: 'the contractor who had written the lower figure' shows several contractors wrote in the tally, so plural possessive. B makes 'tally' a verb clashing with 'recorded'.

tells: Verb-and-object punctuation items are keyed to the unpunctuated option: SEC27A-08 (B), SEC27D-05 (A), SEC27B-01 (B). A test-taker who always picks the plain option wins these, though SEC27B-05 (comma) and SEC27D-09 (colon) break the pattern.

In the 2x2 number-and-tense verb items the key is never the number of the noun right before the blank when that noun differs from the head (A-02, A-07, B-02, B-03, B-07, C-02, C-06, D-02, D-04, D-07, D-08): 'skip the attractor' is reliable but that is the tested rule, not a tell.
Tense in verb items is always settled by one explicit time cue (since, for nine seasons, long-demolished, made obsolete, that autumn); no item requires reading tense from discourse alone.
No positional tell noticed: keys across 40 items are spread over all four letters.

phase2_note: All 40 keys match my cold answers (0 cold misses). Path-coherence failures: SEC27B-10: The explanation rejects B only by claiming the first sentence rules out a restrictive appositive, but that sentence says all cores came from one ship, not that the institute had one ship, and it ignores close apposition ('the ship Kittiwake Star'), which is conventionally unpunctuated. SEC27D-10: The explanation dismisses D as 'neither possessive nor plural' without addressing the noun-adjunct reading 'the contractor tally', which is number-neutral and grammatical. SEC27D-10 is kept despite my phase-1 exclusivity flag: the noun-adjunct reading is weak against the SAT's possessive convention, but a reviewer should look at it. Minor: explanations for C-01/C-04/C-09 reject the no-comma option partly as a missing comma after an introductory element, which is a style point; the garden-path misreading is the real reason, and it holds.
